aib1-the-one-rule.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Would you shout your chatbot question from a billboard? If not, do not paste it into a chatbot. That is the one rule. A vendor chatbot is a stranger's computer: your words travel to a company's servers, where they can be stored, read by a reviewer, and used for training, and pressing delete does not promise they are gone. Here is why.
aib1-the-one-rule.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Would you shout it from a billboard? That is the test for every chatbot question. Since a vendor chatbot is a stranger's computer, treat it as public by default for anything sensitive. Use it freely for ordinary, non-private work; for anything you would not want seen by the highway, keep it out. What is whispered in secret can be shouted from the rooftops (Luke 12:2-3), and the prudent see danger coming and take refuge (Proverbs 22:3). Know where your words go before you send them.

aib2-do-not-share-list.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What should never go into a chatbot? Nine things: who you are (your name tied to your address or birth date), ID numbers, money details, health details, passwords and keys, work secrets, anything from a lawyer, other people's information without their permission, and children's information. Watch hardest for money and for other people's information, where good people slip most. Keeping these out is keeping a trust, your own and your neighbor's (Proverbs 11:13).

aib3-how-the-machine-remembers.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does your chatbot keep, who reads it, and does turning off training erase it? On a consumer tier it keeps your words on its servers, a sample may be read by human reviewers, and your words may train the next model. Turning off training is worth doing, but it generally stops only future use; it does not delete what was already kept, and a short abuse-monitoring window remains. So keep sensitive work for a properly contracted tier, or better, for an A.I. on your own hardware.

aib4-the-law-plain.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which private details lose their protection the moment you paste them? Three stand out. Health information falls outside HIPAA, because a consumer chatbot is not a covered entity and will not sign the contract. A lawyer's material can lose its privilege once shared with a third party. A company secret can lose its trade secret status. The protections you assume do not travel with a paste. This is education, not legal advice.
aib4-the-law-plain.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which private details lose their protection when you paste them into a consumer chatbot? Health information leaves HIPAA's safeguards, a lawyer's communication can lose its privilege, company secrets can forfeit trade secret status and breach an NDA, and identifiers, financial and health data, and student records are regulated under the privacy laws. A chatbot is not a vault. Act with knowledge (Proverbs 13:16), honor the laws that protect people, and when the stakes are real, ask a licensed attorney.

So before you paste anything, run a four-step check: redact it, never paste live secrets, match the tool to how sensitive the work is, and configure what you use. Best of all, keep sensitive work on an A.I. that never leaves your own hardware.
aib6-safe-use-blueprint-sovereign.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Would you hand a stranger your family's records? Then do not paste them raw into a chatbot. Run the card. One, redact and generalize. Four, turn off history and training, knowing off is not the same as erased. When the data never leaves home, there is no stranger to hand it to.
